children.text: Just
15 minutes

from downtown Laoag, the La Paz Sand Dunes are coastal dunes formed by sand carried in by the sea and river and piled up by the wind. Racing up and down the sand ridges by 4x4 jeep, sliding down on a sandboard, and watching the sun set over the South China Sea are the highlights.

The La Paz Sand Dunes spread across the village of La Paz, near the mouth of the Laoag River, on the western coast of Laoag City. Sand carried down by the Laoag River and pushed up by the waves of the South China Sea has been blown by the northeast wind and piled up over the years, forming a landscape of sand ridges tens of meters high separated by hollow valleys. Designated a national geological monument by the Philippine government, it presents a "desert landscape" rarely seen in a tropical island nation.
Ilocos Norte's coastal dunes stretch along the shore from La Paz in Laoag south to Suba in Paoay. Both run 4x4 jeep tours: La Paz is the most accessible, just
15 minutes

from downtown Laoag by tricycle, while Suba pairs well with a visit to Paoay Church. Thanks to their stark, exotic look, these dunes have been used as a filming location many times, in both Philippine and foreign movies.

The star attraction here is unquestionably the 4x4 jeep tour. Modified jeeps race up the sand ridges at full speed and then plunge down steep slopes, a thrill as exciting as a roller coaster that keeps everyone screaming and laughing. The tour also includes stopping midway on a ridge for photos and sandboarding down a steep slope.
It suits adventurous groups of friends, families with children (elementary-school age or older recommended), and photographers alike. Since
1–2 hours
is enough, it's common to combine it with sightseeing in downtown Laoag or a visit to Paoay Church for a full-day itinerary.
The driver speeds up and down the sand ridges, passing through several steep drop sections. Over about
1 hour
, you'll head deep into the dunes, so holding tight to the back-seat handle is a must.

Partway through the tour, you ride a board down a steep slope. If standing is too hard, lying face-down on the board or sitting and sledding down is plenty of fun too. Climbing back up through the sand is more of a workout than you'd expect.
Jump photos against the endless sand ridges and blue sky are the classic shot here. The drivers know all the photography tricks, so just ask and they'll take one for you.
Some operators also rent out ATVs (four-wheeled motorbikes). You can drive one yourself along a designated course, great for anyone who wants to try driving it.
From the western edge of the dunes, you can watch the sun set over the South China Sea. Start your tour after
and you can catch the sunset at the last stop.

The "Sinking Bell Tower," built in the early 17th century and now tilted from ground subsidence, along with St. William's Cathedral and the Ilocos Norte Museum, are all clustered in the city center, making them easy to visit before or after the dunes.
At the mouth of the Laoag River, north of the dunes, you can see where the river meets the sea and watch fishermen's bangka boats. A quiet stroll here offers a different mood from the dunes.

Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific fly from Manila to Laoag International Airport (LAO), about
1 hour 10 minutes
, with one-way fares of roughly
depending on the season. It's
15–20 minutes
from the airport to downtown Laoag by tricycle or taxi, and about
15 minutes
from downtown to the La Paz Sand Dunes.
Buses to Laoag run daily from the Cubao and Sampaloc terminals in Manila, operated by companies such as Partas, Fariñas Trans, and Maria de Leon. The trip takes about
9–11 hours
, with fares of roughly
depending on class. From Vigan, a Laoag-bound bus takes about
2 hours
A tricycle is the easiest way from downtown Laoag to the La Paz Sand Dunes. One-way costs about
, or you can negotiate a round trip with the driver waiting through your tour for about

. A round-trip arrangement is recommended, since it can be hard to find a tricycle back during tour hours. Some 4x4 operators offer packages that include hotel pickup in the city. If you use the Suba dunes on the Paoay side instead, take a Paoay-bound jeepney from Laoag and transfer to a tricycle.
The dune tour is best during the dry season, from
November
to
May
. The sand is dry then, so jeeps climb the ridges well and sandboards slide smoothly. From December to
February
, mornings and evenings are cool and the strong wind carves beautiful ripple patterns into the sand.
From March to
May
, the sand surface gets very hot at midday, making it hard to walk barefoot, and sunlight reflection is intense. During this period, be sure to schedule your tour late in the afternoon, ideally after
During the rainy season from June to
October
, tours can be suspended when it rains, or the sand can get too wet for good sandboarding. From July to
September
, typhoons are frequent, so build extra time into flight and bus schedules. On the other hand, on clear days right after rain, there's less dust and the sky is clean, making for great photos.
Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
There is almost no lodging around the dunes, so staying in downtown Laoag is the norm. The city center has many mid-range hotels and budget pensions priced around

per night. If you want a resort, Fort Ilocandia is a large property beside the dunes south of the city, with a pool and spacious grounds that suit family trips, and it also runs its own dune tour packages.

Laoag is the heartland of Ilocano cuisine. Be sure to try bagnet (pork belly fried twice for a crispy outside and moist inside), pinakbet (vegetables seasoned with bagoong), garlicky Laoag longganisa, and Batac empanada made from rice-flour dough. The empanada stalls around town are busiest in the evening, and dipping the empanada in spicy vinegar is the local way to eat it. For something sweet, try traditional rice cakes like tinubong, made by cooking glutinous rice and coconut milk in a bamboo tube.
The best time to start the tour is
. The sand begins to cool by then, and you can catch the sunset at the end.
Each jeep seats 5–6 people, so if your group is small, you can join with other travelers on the spot and split the cost.
Sand gets into every corner of your clothes and bag. Put your phone in a waterproof pouch or zip-lock bag, and don't change camera lenses while on the sand.
Sunglasses are a must, protecting your eyes from glare and blowing sand.
Closed shoes are better than sandals, though for sandboarding, bare feet are actually more comfortable — just avoid the hot midday sand.
Most places accept cash only. Withdraw money in advance from an ATM in downtown Laoag.
The back seats of the jeep are the most thrilling, while the front seat is relatively comfortable. If you get motion sick easily, ask for a front seat.
Climbing back up the sandy slope after sandboarding is tiring. Bring plenty of water.

The 4x4 tour has many steep drop sections and is not recommended for pregnant women or people with back, neck, or heart conditions. Young children should always be held by a guardian, or check the operator's age policy.
Only use officially licensed operators, and check the safety handles and seat condition before setting off.
At midday from March to
May
, the sand surface is very hot and heatstroke risk is high. Bring a hat, sunscreen, and water, and avoid touring around noon.
The interior of the dunes looks similar everywhere, so it's easy to get lost. Don't wander deep in on your own — stay with the driver.
The dune vegetation holds the sand in place and protects the landscape. Don't trample the grass or leave litter.
Just before the jeep crests a ridge, lean back and hold the handle with both hands. Standing up in excitement is the most dangerous moment.
